name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
description:
Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. Security constructs such as permission levels will often hinder access to information and use of certain techniques, so adversaries will likely need to perform privilege escalation to include use of software exploitation to circumvent those restrictions.

When initially gaining access to a system, an adversary may be operating within a lower privileged process which will prevent them from accessing certain resources on the system. Vulnerabilities may exist, usually in operating system components and software commonly running at higher permissions, that can be exploited to gain higher levels of access on the system. This could enable someone to move from unprivileged or user level permissions to SYSTEM or root permissions depending on the component that is vulnerable. This could also enable an adversary to move from a virtualized environment, such as within a virtual machine or container, onto the underlying host. This may be a necessary step for an adversary compromising an endpoint system that has been properly configured and limits other privilege escalation methods.

Adversaries may bring a signed vulnerable driver onto a compromised machine so that they can exploit the vulnerability to execute code in kernel mode. This process is sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD).(Citation: ESET InvisiMole June 2020)(Citation: Unit42 AcidBox June 2020) Adversaries may include the vulnerable driver with files delivered during Initial Access or download it to a compromised system via [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) or [Lateral Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1570).

Microsoft. (2020, October 15). Microsoft recommended driver block rules. Retrieved March 16, 2021.

telemetry.name: Container Enumeration
telemetry.description: Listing or inspection of container objects.
telemetry.collection_focus: Use authorized Docker API access auditing/instrumentation for list requests; a read-only inventory snapshot gives state but does not prove someone else enumerated containers.

providers.name: Docker Engine events
providers.scope: Daemon lifecycle events for containers and images; collect continuously.

providers.name: Kubernetes API audit
providers.scope: Control-plane context in Kubernetes, not a replacement for runtime observations.

configuration: Subscribe to the lab daemon event stream with filters for the relevant object/action; send it to a durable collector.
Record runtime/container ID, image digest, action, timestamp and host. Join orchestrator identities where available.
Use a protected collector connection. Docker socket access is privileged; never expose it publicly or grant it to the website.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Runtime event history is bounded and can be lost without continuous collection. Image tags are mutable; pin digests. A lifecycle event is not a full process or file audit.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per workload image and namespace: rare process starts, unexpected image/privilege changes and new network relationships. Use workload/deployment identity, not short-lived container IDs alone.

telemetry.name: Driver Load
telemetry.description: Loading of a driver into the running OS.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect Sysmon DriverLoad (6) and retain image path, hash and signature result; distinguish load from file installation.

providers.name: Microsoft Sysmon
providers.scope: Windows event-based collection; enable the event types needed below.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: Linux alternative for supported system-call and file events; different semantics and fields.

providers.name: Apple Endpoint Security clients
providers.scope: macOS alternative where the subscribed event exists; requires an entitled, approved client, not an iOS collector.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Event filtering and sensor versions change coverage. High-volume image-load and process-access collection needs tuning; endpoint events alone do not establish intent.

telemetry.name: Logon Session Creation
telemetry.description: Creation of a logon session with account and logon-type context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Enable Audit Logon and collect successful session creation on the receiving host; join session/logon IDs rather than only account names.

providers.name: Windows Security auditing
providers.scope: Policy-dependent account, object, task and logon records on the host that performs the operation.

configuration: Use a lab-only GPO under Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration. Enable the specific subcategory named below.
For object-level auditing, configure a narrow system access control list (SACL) on the test object in addition to policy. Do not audit an entire production directory by default.

Forward Security events from the responsible host or controller; retain subject and target identities, object identifiers, result and original XML. Confirm effective policy with auditpol /get /category:*.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: A policy checkbox alone does not guarantee an event. Host role, SACL, success/failure selection and audit policy precedence matter. Directory changes may arrive as multiple records.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per principal, host and object: unusual access/request rates, new principal-object relationships, and changes outside approved administration windows. Control for service accounts and scheduled directory maintenance.

telemetry.name: Logon Session Metadata
telemetry.description: Attributes of existing logon sessions and their association with accounts or hosts.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect supported session inventory and correlate session IDs with authentication, logon and logoff events.

providers.name: osquery
providers.scope: Scheduled host-state queries; supported tables and privileges vary by OS. Select a table that actually exposes the required object.

providers.name: Linux Audit plus inventory snapshots
providers.scope: Events explain changes; snapshots describe state at collection time.

configuration: Define the inventory query, allowed host set, interval and least-privileged reader. Store a stable asset ID, observation time and collector version.
Keep successive snapshots and calculate additions, removals and changed attributes. Pair state changes with audit events when available.
Export collector health and missed-poll counts so a missing snapshot is not misclassified as a missing asset.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Snapshots miss short-lived objects and do not identify who caused a change. A generic inventory agent is not guaranteed to expose firmware or kernel-level details.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Compare authorized state snapshots: first-seen drivers/services/modules, unexpected configuration drift and integrity changes. Record collection cadence; absence in a sample is not evidence of deletion.

telemetry.name: Module Load
telemetry.description: A module or library being loaded into a running process.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon ImageLoad (7) to lab processes/paths; retain module hash, signer and destination process. Inventory alone does not prove a module loaded.

atlas_basic.title: T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
atlas_basic.logic: MATCH(exploit_mitigation_alert OR known_local_exploit_signature) -> ALERT; SEQUENCE(unprivileged_process, privileged_child_process) WITHIN 1m -> ALERT

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

analytics.name: Analytic 1419
analytics.guidance: Detects exploitation attempts targeting vulnerable kernel drivers or OS components, often followed by unusual process or token behavior.

tuning.description: Targeted BYOVD drivers may vary based on campaign and tooling.
Controls temporal linking of driver load → process spawn → privilege use.
Parent-child relationships vary by exploitation vector (e.g., LOLBin vs. dropper).

analytics.name: Analytic 1420
analytics.guidance: Detects escalation via vulnerable setuid binaries or kernel modules, often chained with unusual access to /proc/kallsyms or /dev/kmem.

tuning.description: Legitimate SUID binaries vary across distributions; false positives may arise.
Allows chaining kernel module load with privilege spike or privilege-sensitive process activity.
Default is uid=0, but environments may vary with containerized root-like accounts.

analytics.name: Analytic 1421
analytics.guidance: Detects use of vulnerable kernel extensions or entitlements abused via setuid or AppleScript injection chains.

tuning.description: Entitlements vary by app and OS version; some allow unexpected behavior.
Correlate SUID execution or AppleScript injection with privilege gain or module load.

analytics.name: Analytic 1422
analytics.guidance: Detects container breakout behavior via exploitation (e.g., DirtyPipe, CVE-2022-0847), followed by host OS interaction or escalated capability assignment.

tuning.description: May vary with CVE technique or custom syscall wrapper.
Controls correlation of breakout → host interaction.

mitigations.name: Threat Intelligence Program
mitigations.description: Develop a robust cyber threat intelligence capability to determine what types and levels of threat may use software exploits and 0-days against a particular organization.

mitigations.name: Execution Prevention
mitigations.description: Consider blocking the execution of known vulnerable drivers that adversaries may exploit to execute code in kernel mode. Validate driver block rules in audit mode to ensure stability prior to production deployment.(Citation: Microsoft Driver Block Rules)

references.description: Microsoft. (2020, October 15). Microsoft recommended driver block rules. Retrieved March 16, 2021.

mitigations.name: Application Isolation and Sandboxing
mitigations.description: Make it difficult for adversaries to advance their operation through exploitation of undiscovered or unpatched vulnerabilities by using sandboxing. Other types of virtualization and application microsegmentation may also mitigate the impact of some types of exploitation. Risks of additional exploits and weaknesses in these systems may still exist. (Citation: Ars Technica Pwn2Own 2017 VM Escape)

references.description: Goodin, D. (2017, March 17). Virtual machine escape fetches $105,000 at Pwn2Own hacking contest - updated. Retrieved March 12, 2018.

mitigations.name: Exploit Protection
mitigations.description: Security applications that look for behavior used during exploitation such as Windows Defender Exploit Guard (WDEG) and the Enhanced Mitigation Experience Toolkit (EMET) can be used to mitigate some exploitation behavior. (Citation: TechNet Moving Beyond EMET) Control flow integrity checking is another way to potentially identify and stop a software exploit from occurring. (Citation: Wikipedia Control Flow Integrity) Many of these protections depend on the architecture and target application binary for compatibility and may not work for software components targeted for privilege escalation.

references.description: Nunez, N. (2017, August 9). Moving Beyond EMET II – Windows Defender Exploit Guard. Retrieved March 12, 2018.
Wikipedia. (2018, January 11). Control-flow integrity. Retrieved March 12, 2018.

mitigations.name: Update Software
mitigations.description: Update software regularly by employing patch management for internal enterprise endpoints and servers.
